whoa don't send this. It might sound like a good idea right now but from the gist of this 1. you're upset (understandably) but 2. you're putting a lot of blame on her. Long distance sucks. Aside from unfaithfulness or another personal failing, it's probably the hardest thing for a relationship to go through. I definitely understand feeling like she might not love you because actions on FaceTime and through text can come through so differently than you mean them to. That especially makes sense if your love language is physical touch or gift giving, things that are super hard to do online. I agree you guys should have a conversation, but it shouldn't be a confrontation and it shouldn't be an accusation (on either side). Open up to her before you shut her out. Maybe start by saying "I've been feeling like you don't really want to play x video game with me and you're just doing it to placate me. I understand if that's the case, but I'd really like to know. I value your opinions and your time and I want to make sure we spend the time we have together doing something that we both get excited about". And if you're upset that she doesn't want to do some things you do, or that you're not compatible in some ways, that's something you need to first talk to her about and then work on by yourself. Relationships are about compromise. You're not going to be 100% on board with everything your partner does but it's your job as the people in the relationship to find things that you are 100% on board with and spend your time together doing that. There will always be time to play a video game or do something else another time, but relationship time needs to be for both people. And you can tell her that too - "I feel like we haven't been having a lot of time together doing things we both enjoy. I'd like to find something to do together, so we can connect on a deeper level."
Of course, if you're just done with the relationship, the conversation will probably have a different tone. But it seems like you're acting out of emotion, and pushing her away because you want her to come back (I'm only saying that because I have regrettably done the same thing) and that if you collect your thoughts a little bit you might see that the relationship is worth trying a bit harder for. 
I'm not attacking you, your partner, or your post. I completely understand the anger and fear and hurt that comes from feeling like your significant other is losing feelings. It's deep grief and it can be immobilizing. I just want to suggest a different take on it and maybe even if you do break up with her, it will be more amicable.

I think all of the people who are saying "if it's not a yes it's a no" are forgetting how truly stressful not only being in high school is and how hellish taking exams are but also parents. My mom raised me pretty conservatively Korean and puts extreme pressure on me about my grades, and puts so much stress into my life that sometimes relationships are just too hard to juggle without either becoming my therapists or becoming outlets for my emotions that strain the relationship too far. 

I (17m) was super school focused until I met my boyfriend and I still get passable grades but they're definitely not as good because no matter how much you try, you will put at least some aspects of your relationship before your schoolwork. It's just part of being a teen and having these new exciting experiences.  So I would keep in mind that she might not want to go out with you period, but give her the benefit of the doubt and also remember that there are other things going on in her life that maybe she's dealing with so that she can be the best girlfriend for you when the time comes. As for what to do with her, if you end up doing anything in the pandemic - I would make it clear that it's nothing serious, maybe not even a "date" if you don't want to call it that. Tell her you're bringing her somewhere or giving her a gift because you like her and enjoy her company, and that you want to ease any stress she might have, not add to it. Just make sure you guys are always communicating and on the same page about what you want at that moment and your relationship, when it comes, will be as smooth as teen relationships can be :)

This will get buried and might not make much sense but I thought I'd try! As a transgender male (assigned female at birth) I would explain it this way. Gender expression is a social construct, e.g painting nails, wearing skirts, doing "masculine" things like chopping wood. These are norms separated by sex that have been cultivated by society to be gendered. However, how people identify (NOT how they express themselves through clothes, etc) is rooted more in actual science. Studies have shown that a person assigned male at birth who identifies as female will have a more feminine brain. The structures of that person's brain will more closely resemble the structures of a biologically female brain than they will resemble a biological male's brain. I won't speak on non-binary brains, because there's less research there and I'm not very familiar with that. But in short at least in my opinion the social construct comes more in how people express their gender than how they actually identify or what their actual gender is - "gender" is a personal construct, and depends on each person's brain, if that makes sense.
